notes.front: What is the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model?
notes.back: An international reference model that splits communication between open systems into seven layers, from Physical (layer 1) up to Application (layer 7).
notes.explanation: Each layer offers services to the layer above it and relies on the services of the layer below.
notes.example: Like a postal chain in which writer, sorter, van driver and depot each do one job and hand on to the next.
notes.source: ITU-T Recommendation X.200 (07/1994), Basic Reference Model, 6.1 and 6.3, PDF p. 32
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the TCP/IP model, as SP 800-77 describes it?
notes.back: The four-layer model of IP networking, the standard used throughout the world for network communications.
notes.explanation: SP 800-77 notes that the name covers more than just the Transmission Control Protocol.
notes.example: Like the OSI model, but with four broader layers instead of seven.
notes.evidence: IP networking (sometimes called TCP/IP, although it encompasses more than just TCP, the Transmission Control Protocol) is the standard used throughout the world to provide network communications. IP communications are roughly composed of four layers that work together.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, 2.1 The Need for Network Layer Security, PDF p. 20

notes.front: What is Internet Protocol version 6 (IPv6)?
notes.back: The newer version of the Internet Protocol that is replacing IPv4, whose address space is almost exhausted.
notes.explanation: IPv6 is not backwards compatible with IPv4, so organisations must change their network infrastructure and systems to deploy it.
notes.example: Like moving a country to longer phone numbers: far more numbers, but old equipment has to be changed.
notes.evidence: The migration to IPv6 services is inevitable as the IPv4 address space is almost exhausted. IPv6 is not backwards compatible with IPv4, which means organizations will have to change their network infrastructure and systems to deploy IPv6.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-119, Guidelines for the Secure Deployment of IPv6, Executive Summary, PDF p. 10

notes.front: What is an anycast address?
notes.back: An address shared by several interfaces; a packet sent to it goes to one of them, usually the closest as routing decides.
notes.explanation: Anycast was added on to IPv4 but was designed as a basic component of IPv6.
notes.example: Like a national helpline number that connects each caller to the nearest call centre.
notes.evidence: Addresses that can identify several interfaces on one or more nodes; a packet with an anycast destination address is delivered to one of the interfaces bearing the address, usually the closest one as determined by routing protocols. Anycast addressing was introduced as an add-on for IPv4, but it was designed as a basic component of IPv6.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-119, Guidelines for the Secure Deployment of IPv6, 3.1.3 IPv6 Address Types, PDF p. 29

notes.front: What is Internet Protocol Security (IPsec)?
notes.back: A framework of open standards for ensuring private communications over IP networks.
notes.explanation: It has become the most commonly used network layer security control for protecting communications.
notes.example: Like sealing every lorry that leaves a depot, whatever it carries, instead of asking each sender to lock their own parcel.
notes.evidence: IPsec has emerged as the most commonly used network layer security control for protecting communications. IPsec is a framework of open standards for ensuring private communications over IP networks.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, 2.2 The IPsec Protocol, PDF p. 23

notes.front: What is the Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP)?
notes.back: The IPsec protocol that carries the encrypted and integrity-protected network communications across the network.
notes.explanation: If only integrity protection is needed, ESP can run with null encryption.
notes.example: Like an opaque, tamper-evident envelope put round each packet's contents.
notes.evidence: Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) is the protocol that transports the encrypted and integrity-protected network communications across the network. If only integrity protection is needed without encryption, the ESP protocol can use NULL encryption.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, Executive Summary, PDF p. 8

notes.front: What is Internet Key Exchange (IKE)?
notes.back: The protocol IPsec uses to negotiate connection settings and session keys and to authenticate the endpoints to each other.
notes.explanation: It also manages, updates and deletes IPsec-protected channels; the current version is IKEv2.
notes.example: Like two diplomats agreeing the code book and checking each other's credentials before any letters are exchanged.
notes.evidence: Internet Key Exchange (IKE) is the protocol used by IPsec to negotiate IPsec connection settings; authenticate endpoints to each other; define the security parameters of IPsec-protected connections; negotiate session keys; and manage, update, and delete IPsec-protected communication channels. The current version is IKEv2.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, Executive Summary, PDF p. 8

notes.front: What is a virtual private network (VPN)?
notes.back: A virtual network built on top of existing physical networks, giving a secure channel for data and control information between computers or networks.
notes.explanation: IPsec is typically used to encrypt traffic between hosts and to create one.
notes.example: Like an armoured van on public roads: the road is shared, the cargo is protected.
notes.evidence: typically used to encrypt Internet Protocol (IP) traffic between hosts in a network and to create a virtual private network (VPN). A VPN is a virtual network built on top of existing physical networks that provides a secure communications mechanism for data and control information transmitted between computers or networks.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, Executive Summary, PDF p. 7

notes.front: What is Transport Layer Security (TLS)?
notes.back: A protocol that provides a protected channel for sending data between a server and a client.
notes.explanation: The client is often, but not always, a web browser.
notes.example: Like a sealed pneumatic tube between a bank teller and a customer's window.
notes.evidence: TLS provides a protected channel for sending data between a server and a client. The client is often, but not always, a web browser.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-52 Rev. 2, Guidelines for the Selection, Configuration, and Use of TLS Implementations, 1 Introduction, PDF p. 10

notes.front: What is Secure Sockets Layer (SSL)?
notes.back: The precursor protocol to TLS: TLS is based on SSL 3.0 and considered an improvement to it.
notes.explanation: The first version under the TLS name, TLS 1.0, is specified in RFC 2246.
notes.example: Like an older model of lock that today's lock was developed from.
notes.evidence: TLS is based on a precursor protocol called the Secure Sockets Layer Version 3.0 (SSL 3.0) and is considered to be an improvement to SSL 3.0. SSL 3.0 is specified in [32]. The Transport Layer Security version 1 (TLS 1.0) is specified in Request for Comments (RFC) 2246
notes.source: NIST SP 800-52 Rev. 2, Guidelines for the Selection, Configuration, and Use of TLS Implementations, Abstract, PDF p. 5

notes.front: What is Secure Shell (SSH)?
notes.back: A widely used application layer protocol suite, often used for secure remote login and secure file transfer.
notes.explanation: It can also tunnel specific ports through an SSH connection.
notes.example: Like a private, locked intercom to a distant machine's console that can also carry other lines through it.
notes.evidence: SSH is a commonly used application layer protocol suite. While it is often used as a secure remote login application and a secure file transfer application, it can also be used to tunnel specific ports via an SSH connection
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, 8.4 Secure Shell (SSH), PDF p. 107

notes.front: What is the Internet Small Computer Systems Interface (iSCSI)?
notes.back: A protocol for building a storage area network over a possibly shared local or wide area network.
notes.explanation: The other kind of storage area network SP 800-209 describes uses a specialised high-speed network such as Fibre Channel.
notes.example: Like reaching a disk in another building as though it were plugged into your own machine.
notes.evidence: uses a specialized, high-speed network (e.g., Fibre-Channel) that provides block-level access to storage. Another implementation of a SAN uses the Internet Small Computer Systems Interface (iSCSI) protocol over a possibly shared LAN/WAN infrastructure.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-209, Security Guidelines for Storage Infrastructure, 1 Introduction, PDF p. 11

notes.front: In this deck, what is a converged protocol?
notes.back: A specialised protocol, such as a storage protocol, run over or encapsulated within common networking protocols such as TCP/IP or Ethernet.
notes.explanation: SP 800-209 does not use the term 'converged protocol'; it describes storage protocols, such as iSCSI over TCP/IP and Fibre Channel over IP or Ethernet, running this way. The wider definition is the deck's.
notes.example: Like sending goods through the ordinary postal network instead of running a private courier fleet.
notes.evidence: storage-specific protocols running over (or encapsulated within) common networking protocols (e.g., iSCSI by design running over Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol (TCP/IP), Fibre-Channel over IP [FCIP], Fibre-Channel over Ethernet (FCoE), cloud block storage)
notes.source: NIST SP 800-209, Security Guidelines for Storage Infrastructure, 2.1 Storage Technologies, PDF p. 15

notes.front: What is Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP)?
notes.back: Carrying voice as traffic over an IP data connection.
notes.explanation: SP 800-187 compares mobile-network voice, which crosses the network over the data connection, to VoIP.
notes.example: Like sending a phone call as a stream of small data parcels rather than over its own line.
notes.evidence: voice traffic traverses the network over the data connection using protocols, such as VoLTE, which is similar to Voice Over IP (VoIP).
notes.source: NIST SP 800-187, Guide to LTE Security, 2 Overview of LTE Technology, PDF p. 11

notes.front: What is the management plane, as SP 800-209 uses the idea for storage?
notes.back: The protocols, operations and network access used to create and destroy devices, configure their attributes and map them to hosts.
notes.explanation: SP 800-209 calls it the data management plane and sets it beside the data consumption plane, which carries the I/O itself; how far the two are separated is a design choice.
notes.example: Like a building's control room, kept apart from the corridors that visitors walk through.
notes.evidence: the I/O operations themselves, and the physical and logical network connections used to perform such operations. “Data management plane” - includes protocols, operations and network access used to create and destroy the device, to configure its attributes, to map it to hosts, etc.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-209, Security Guidelines for Storage Infrastructure, 3.4 Data Planes, PDF p. 40

notes.front: What is east-west traffic?
notes.back: Traffic that stays within the local network, such as server-to-server traffic.
notes.explanation: SP 800-215 says over 75% of network traffic is now east-west, much of it because applications are built from microservices.
notes.example: Like post sent between departments inside one office, never leaving the building.
notes.evidence: over 75 % of network traffic is now east-west (i.e., within the local network) or server-to-server (due to applications being based on microservices)
notes.source: NIST SP 800-215, Guide to a Secure Enterprise Network Landscape, 2 Traditional Network Security Approaches, PDF p. 14

notes.front: What is out-of-band management?
notes.back: Administering systems over out-of-band channels: paths separate from the ones that carry routine operational traffic.
notes.explanation: SP 800-53 defines the channels, such as local non-network access or physically separate network paths; using them to administer systems is what makes the management out-of-band.
notes.example: Like a caretaker's private back stair to the plant room, used instead of crossing the busy public lobby.
notes.evidence: Out-of-band channels include local, non-network accesses to systems; network paths physically separate from network paths used for operational traffic; or non-electronic paths, such as the U.S. Postal Service. The use of out-of-band channels is contrasted with the use of in-band channels (i.e., the same channels) that carry routine operational traffic.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, SC-37 Out-of-Band Channels, PDF p. 350

notes.front: What is an air gap?
notes.back: Leaving devices physically unconnected when they have no business need to communicate.
notes.explanation: SP 800-82 gives this as guidance for devices that do not need to talk to each other.
notes.example: Like a filing cabinet in a room with no doorway to the rest of the building.
notes.evidence: Devices that do not have a business need to communicate should not be connected (i.e., air gapped).
notes.source: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security, Appendix F, SC-7, PDF p. 246

notes.front: What is a virtual local area network (VLAN)?
notes.back: A logical separation of areas within a network, set up on switches by port, used when physical separation is not feasible.
notes.explanation: Cost or other prohibitive measures can make physical separation infeasible.
notes.example: Like painting coloured lanes in one warehouse so teams stay apart without building walls.
notes.evidence: A VLAN can be used to logically separate areas within a network when physical separation may not be feasible due to cost or other prohibitive measures. VLANs are implemented on modern network switching equipment that logically separates network traffic based on switch ports.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security, E.1.3 Virtual Local Area Networks, PDF p. 224

notes.front: What is micro-segmentation in a zero trust architecture?
notes.back: Placing individual resources, or small groups of them, on their own network segment protected by a gateway security component.
notes.explanation: The protecting device can be an intelligent switch or router, a next-generation firewall or a special-purpose gateway.
notes.example: Like giving every office its own locked door and guard, instead of one guard at the building entrance.
notes.evidence: An enterprise may choose to implement a ZTA based on placing individual or groups of resources on a unique network segment protected by a gateway security component. In this approach, the enterprise places infrastructure devices such as intelligent switches (or routers) or next generation firewalls (NGFWs) or special purpose gateway devices
notes.source: NIST SP 800-207, Zero Trust Architecture, 3.1.2 ZTA Using Micro-Segmentation, PDF p. 21

notes.front: What is an overlay network, in SP 800-125B's virtual networking?
notes.back: Virtual networking in which isolation comes from encapsulating the Ethernet frames that virtual machines send.
notes.explanation: Several encapsulation, or overlay, schemes can be used to do this.
notes.example: Like sealing a letter inside a courier's envelope that carries its own delivery label.
notes.evidence: In overlay-based virtual networking, isolation is realized by encapsulating an Ethernet frame received from a VM. Various encapsulation schemes (or overlay schemes) can be used
notes.source: NIST SP 800-125B, Secure Virtual Network Configuration for Virtual Machine (VM) Protection, 2.5 Using Overlay-Based Virtual Networking, PDF p. 15

notes.front: What is egress filtering?
notes.back: Filtering outgoing network traffic; filtering incoming traffic is called ingress filtering.
notes.explanation: It lets organisations restrict internal traffic, for example blocking external file transfer servers or stopping denial of service attacks launched from inside against outsiders.
notes.example: Like a security desk that checks bags on the way out, not only on the way in.
notes.evidence: Filtering inbound traffic is known as ingress filtering. Outgoing traffic can also be filtered, a process referred to as egress filtering. Here, organizations can implement restrictions on their internal traffic, such as blocking the use of external file transfer protocol (FTP) servers or preventing denial of service (DoS) attacks from being launched from within the organization against outside entities.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, 2.1 Firewall Technologies, PDF p. 13

notes.front: What is a wireless local area network (WLAN)?
notes.back: A group of wireless networking devices within a limited area, such as an office building, that exchange data by radio.
notes.explanation: WLAN technologies are based on the 802.11 standard and its amendments.
notes.example: Like a wired office network, but with the cables replaced by radio.
notes.evidence: A wireless local area network (WLAN) is a group of wireless networking devices within a limited geographic area, such as an office building, that exchange data through radio communications. WLAN technologies are based on the IEEE 802.11 standard and its amendments.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-153, Guidelines for Securing Wireless Local Area Networks (WLANs), Executive Summary, PDF p. 6

notes.front: What is Bluetooth?
notes.back: An open standard for short-range radio communication, used mainly to form wireless personal area networks.
notes.explanation: It is built into many business and consumer devices, from phones and laptops to cars, medical devices and headsets.
notes.example: Like a short cable between a phone and a headset, but made of radio.
notes.evidence: Bluetooth is an open standard for short-range radio frequency (RF) communication. Bluetooth wireless technology is used primarily to establish wireless personal area networks (WPANs). Bluetooth has been integrated into many types of business and consumer devices, including cell phones, laptops, automobiles, medical devices, printers, keyboards, mice, headsets
notes.source: NIST SP 800-121 Rev. 2 (upd. 1), Guide to Bluetooth Security, Executive Summary, PDF p. 6

notes.front: What is Long Term Evolution (LTE)?
notes.back: Fourth-generation (4G) cellular technology, a main driver of mobile networks becoming many people's main way onto the internet.
notes.explanation: SP 800-187 notes cellular technology has become the primary portal to the internet for a large part of the population.
notes.example: Like a Wi-Fi network run by a mobile operator across a whole country.
notes.evidence: Cellular technology plays an increasingly large role in society as it has become the primary portal to the internet for a large segment of the population. One of the main drivers making this change possible is the deployment of 4th generation (4G) Long Term Evolution (LTE) cellular technologies.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-187, Guide to LTE Security, Abstract, PDF p. 4

notes.front: What is Zigbee, as NIST IR 8259 lists it?
notes.back: A network interface technology an IoT device can use to connect to the digital world, listed beside Ethernet, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and LTE.
notes.explanation: NIST IR 8259 counts at least one such network interface among the parts of an IoT device.
notes.example: Like the Wi-Fi card in a laptop: one of several kinds of network interface a small connected device might carry.
notes.evidence: at least one network interface (e.g., Ethernet, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Long-Term Evolution (LTE), Zigbee, Ultra-Wideband (UWB)) for interfacing with the digital world.
notes.source: NIST IR 8259r1, Foundational Cybersecurity Activities for IoT Product Manufacturers, 1 Introduction, PDF p. 9

notes.front: What is a content distribution network (CDN), and what does SP 800-209 expect of its copies?
notes.back: A network that serves cached copies of content; the copies should keep at least the security characteristics of the source data.
notes.explanation: SP 800-209 puts such cached copies alongside replicas and proxies; it spells the name 'content delivery network'.
notes.example: Like branch libraries holding copies of popular books so readers need not travel to the central library.
notes.evidence: Cached copies (e.g., using content delivery network (CDN), replicas, and proxies) retaining at least the same security characteristics as the source data.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-209, Security Guidelines for Storage Infrastructure, 4.4 Data Protection, PDF p. 55

notes.front: What is software-defined networking (SDN)?
notes.back: Networking that keeps packet forwarding (the data plane) at the switch and moves routing decisions (the control plane) to a central controller.
notes.explanation: Traditional switches do both jobs: forwarding packets and running the distributed routing algorithms.
notes.example: Like air traffic control guiding many aircraft from one tower, instead of each pilot planning routes alone.
notes.evidence: Traditional networking switches are responsible for both forwarding packets (data plane) and running the distributed algorithms that determine routing (control plane). SDN is a technology that evolves this concept by keeping the data plane at the switch and moving the control plane to a centralized controller.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security, E.1.4 Software-Defined Networking, PDF p. 225

notes.front: What is a software-defined wide-area network (SD-WAN)?
notes.back: Wide area networking that decouples the control plane from the data plane and lets policies be specified centrally.
notes.explanation: The centrally set policies include access control, routing and application traffic prioritisation.
notes.example: Like SDN, but applied to the links that join an organisation's distant sites.
notes.evidence: software-defined wide area network (SD-WAN). SD-WAN technology removes the tight coupling between the control plane and data plane functions of the network and enables the centralized specification of various policies, such as access control, routing, and application traffic prioritization.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-215, Guide to a Secure Enterprise Network Landscape, 5.3 Secure Access Service Edge, PDF p. 32

notes.front: What is a virtual private cloud (VPC)?
notes.back: A private virtual network that a cloud customer configures inside the provider's native network, in which its compute resources are provisioned.
notes.explanation: SP 800-215 counts such networks as part of today's enterprise network, beside on-premises networks.
notes.example: Like renting a fenced plot inside a large shared business park.
notes.evidence: The private virtual networks that the enterprise (cloud services subscriber) configures in the cloud service provider’s native network within which its compute resources will be provisioned (e.g., virtual network [VNet], virtual private cloud [VPC]) • Various local networks on enterprise premises
notes.source: NIST SP 800-215, Guide to a Secure Enterprise Network Landscape, 1 Introduction, PDF p. 10

notes.front: Which OSI layer gives the mechanical and electrical means to set up, keep and release the physical connections that carry bits?
notes.back: The Physical Layer (layer 1).
notes.explanation: It passes bit streams transparently between the data link entities above it.
notes.source: ITU-T Recommendation X.200 (07/1994), Basic Reference Model, 7.7.2 Purpose (Physical Layer), PDF p. 53
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which OSI layer detects, and may correct, errors that arise in the Physical Layer?
notes.back: The Data Link Layer (layer 2).
notes.explanation: A data link connection is built on one or more physical connections, which is where those errors arise.
notes.source: ITU-T Recommendation X.200 (07/1994), Basic Reference Model, 7.6.2 Purpose (Data Link Layer), PDF p. 50
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which OSI layer frees the transport layer from any concern with routing and relaying?
notes.back: The Network Layer (layer 3).
notes.explanation: It provides connection-mode or connectionless transmission among transport entities, and sets up and ends network connections between open systems.
notes.source: ITU-T Recommendation X.200 (07/1994), Basic Reference Model, 7.5.2 Purpose (Network Layer), PDF p. 45
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which OSI layer gives the session layer transparent data transfer, sparing it the details of reliable, cost-effective delivery?
notes.back: The Transport Layer (layer 4).
notes.explanation: It gets the most out of the network below, giving each session the performance it needs as cheaply as possible.
notes.source: ITU-T Recommendation X.200 (07/1994), Basic Reference Model, 7.4.2 Purpose (Transport Layer), PDF p. 41
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which OSI layer lets cooperating presentation entities organise and synchronise their dialogue?
notes.back: The Session Layer (layer 5).
notes.explanation: It opens the session, keeps the back-and-forth of data orderly and closes the session cleanly at the end.
notes.source: ITU-T Recommendation X.200 (07/1994), Basic Reference Model, 7.3.2 Purpose (Session Layer), PDF p. 39
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which OSI layer gives application entities a common representation of the data they exchange?
notes.back: The Presentation Layer (layer 6).
notes.explanation: That spares the applications any concern with how information is represented, giving them syntax independence.
notes.source: ITU-T Recommendation X.200 (07/1994), Basic Reference Model, 7.2.2 Purpose (Presentation Layer), PDF p. 37
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which OSI layer is an application process's only way into the OSI environment?
notes.back: The Application Layer (layer 7).
notes.explanation: As the highest layer, it has no layer above it to serve.
notes.source: ITU-T Recommendation X.200 (07/1994), Basic Reference Model, 7.1.2 (Application Layer), PDF p. 36
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which layer of SP 800-77's four-layer IP model sends and receives data for particular applications, such as the Domain Name System?
notes.back: The application layer.
notes.explanation: Web traffic over the Hypertext Transfer Protocol is another of its examples.
notes.evidence: Application Layer. This layer sends and receives data for particular applications, such as Domain Name System (DNS), web traffic via the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP)
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, 2.1 The Need for Network Layer Security, PDF p. 20

notes.front: Which layer of the IP model provides connection-oriented or connectionless transport for application-layer services?
notes.back: The transport layer.
notes.explanation: The Transmission Control Protocol gives reliable connection-oriented communications; the User Datagram Protocol gives unreliable connectionless ones.
notes.evidence: Transport Layer. This layer provides connection-oriented or connectionless services for transporting application-layer services between networks. The transport layer can optionally assure the reliability of communications. TCP, which provides reliable connection-oriented communications, and the User Datagram Protocol (UDP), which provides unreliable connectionless communications
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, 2.1 The Need for Network Layer Security, PDF p. 20

notes.front: Which layer of the IP model routes packets across networks?
notes.back: The network layer.
notes.explanation: IP is its fundamental protocol; the Internet Control Message Protocol and Internet Group Management Protocol also work there.
notes.evidence: Network Layer. This layer routes packets across networks. IP is the fundamental network layer protocol for TCP/IP. Other commonly used protocols at the network layer are the Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) and the Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP).
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, 2.1 The Need for Network Layer Security, PDF p. 20

notes.front: Which layer of the IP model handles communications between the physical network components?
notes.back: The data link layer.
notes.explanation: Its best-known protocols are Ethernet and the 802.11 Wi-Fi standards.
notes.evidence: Data Link Layer. This layer handles communications between the physical network components. The best-known data link layer protocols are Ethernet and the various Wireless Fidelity (WiFi) standards such as the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) 802.11.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, 2.1 The Need for Network Layer Security, PDF p. 20

notes.front: According to RFC 1122, what end-to-end delivery guarantee does IP itself give?
notes.back: None: a packet can be lost, corrupted, repeated or delivered in the wrong order.
notes.explanation: IP forwards each packet on its own, with no connection set up, so any reliability has to come from the protocols above it, such as TCP.
notes.source: RFC 1122, Requirements for Internet Hosts: Communication Layers, 1.1.3 Internet Protocol Suite (Internet Layer), page 10
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why can a security control at a higher layer not fully protect the lower layers?
notes.back: The lower layers perform functions that the higher layers are not aware of.
notes.explanation: Data passes down from the highest layer to the lowest, each layer adding more information that controls above it never see.
notes.evidence: As previously explained, data is passed from the highest to the lowest layer, with each layer adding more information. Therefore, a security control at a higher layer cannot provide full protection for lower layers because the lower layers perform functions of which the higher layers are not aware.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, 2.1 The Need for Network Layer Security, PDF p. 21

notes.front: A TLS connection links two email servers. What does it not protect, according to SP 800-77?
notes.back: The message content against manipulation by either email server; TLS gives transport security, not data origin security.
notes.explanation: It does protect the transport itself from eavesdroppers.
notes.evidence: The transport layer can only provide transport security, not data origin security. For example, a TLS-based connection between two email servers protects the transport from eavesdroppers but does not protect the message content transmitted within that TLS connection from manipulation by one of the two email servers.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, 2.1 The Need for Network Layer Security, PDF p. 21

notes.front: What can network layer controls such as IPsec protect that transport layer controls cannot?
notes.back: The IP information, such as IP addresses, for each packet, as well as the data within the packets.
notes.explanation: IP information is added at the network layer, so controls there can cover it.
notes.evidence: Another advantage of network layer controls is that since IP information (e.g., IP addresses) is added at this layer, the controls can protect both the data within the packets and the IP information for each packet.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, 2.1 The Need for Network Layer Security, PDF p. 22

notes.front: How long are IPv4 and IPv6 addresses?
notes.back: IPv4: 32 bits. IPv6: 128 bits.
notes.explanation: An IPv6 address is written as eight 16-bit fields in colon-delimited hexadecimal; an IPv4 address as four decimal numbers.
notes.evidence: Each IPv4 address is typically 32 bits long and is written as four decimal numbers representing 8-bit octets and separated by decimal points or periods. An example address is 172.30.128.97. Each IPv6 address is 128 bits long (as defined in RFC 4291) and is written as eight 16-bit fields in colon-delimited hexadecimal notation
notes.source: NIST SP 800-119, Guidelines for the Secure Deployment of IPv6, 2.3.1 Extended Address Space, PDF p. 17

notes.front: What happened to broadcast in IPv6?
notes.back: It was eliminated; multicast takes on a much larger role instead.
notes.explanation: Multicast also works with neighbour and router discovery on the local link for stateless address autoconfiguration and address resolution.
notes.evidence: In IPv6, broadcast has been eliminated and multicast takes on a much larger role. In addition to replacing broadcast, it also works with ICMPv6 neighbor discovery and router discovery on the local link to perform stateless address autoconfiguration and address resolution.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-119, Guidelines for the Secure Deployment of IPv6, 4.2 Multicast, PDF p. 68

notes.front: In IPv6, what is a unicast address?
notes.back: An address that identifies one interface on a single node; a packet sent to it is delivered to that interface.
notes.explanation: It is the one-to-one address type, set beside multicast and anycast in IPv6.
notes.evidence: Unicast Addresses. Addresses that identify one interface on a single node; a packet with a unicast destination address is delivered to that interface.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-119, Guidelines for the Secure Deployment of IPv6, 3.1.3 IPv6 Address Types, PDF p. 29

notes.front: In IPv6, what is a multicast address?
notes.back: An identifier for a set of interfaces, typically on different nodes; a packet sent to it is delivered to all of them.
notes.explanation: Multicast addresses exist in IPv4 too, but in IPv6 multicasting has new applications.
notes.evidence: An identifier for a set of interfaces (typically belonging to different nodes). A packet sent to a multicast address is delivered to all interfaces identified by that address.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-119, Guidelines for the Secure Deployment of IPv6, 3.1.3 IPv6 Address Types, PDF p. 29

notes.front: What should an organisation that is not yet deploying IPv6 do with IPv6 traffic at its firewall, according to SP 800-119?
notes.back: Block all IPv6 traffic, native and tunnelled, both incoming and outgoing.
notes.explanation: The block covers tunnelled IPv6 as well as native IPv6, in both directions.
notes.evidence: Block all IPv6 traffic, native and tunneled, at the organization's firewall. Both incoming and outgoing traffic should be blocked.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-119, Guidelines for the Secure Deployment of IPv6, Executive Summary, PDF p. 11

notes.front: What does IPsec's peer authentication ensure?
notes.back: Each endpoint confirms the other's identity, so traffic goes only to the expected, authorised endpoint.
notes.explanation: It is one of the protections IPsec can give, depending on how it is implemented and configured.
notes.evidence: Peer Authentication. Each IPsec endpoint confirms the identity of the other IPsec endpoint with which it wishes to communicate, ensuring that the network traffic and data is only transmitted to the expected and authorized endpoint.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, 2.2 The IPsec Protocol, PDF p. 23

notes.front: What does IPsec's replay protection prevent?
notes.back: The same data being accepted more than once, or grossly out of order.
notes.explanation: That stops attackers copying valid IPsec-encrypted data and sending it again for malicious purposes.
notes.evidence: Replay Protection. The same data will not be accepted multiple times, and data is not accepted grossly out of order. This prevents attackers from copying and retransmitting valid IPsec encrypted data for malicious purposes.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, 2.2 The IPsec Protocol, PDF p. 24

notes.front: Which IPsec VPN architecture protects communications between two specific networks, such as a main office and a branch office?
notes.back: Gateway-to-gateway.
notes.explanation: Two business partners' networks are SP 800-77's other example of such a pair.
notes.evidence: Gateway-to-gateway. This architecture protects communications between two specific networks, such as an organization’s main office network and a branch office network or two business partners’ networks.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, Executive Summary, PDF p. 8

notes.front: Which VPN architecture, also known as host-to-gateway, protects communications between individual hosts and an organisation's network?
notes.back: Remote access.
notes.explanation: It is most often used so that hosts on unsecured networks, such as travelling staff and teleworkers, can reach internal services.
notes.evidence: Remote access. Also known as host-to-gateway, this architecture protects communications between one or more individual hosts and a specific network belonging to an organization. The remote access architecture is most often used to allow hosts on unsecured networks, such as traveling employees and telecommuters, to gain access to internal organizational services
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, Executive Summary, PDF p. 8

notes.front: Which parts of the path does a gateway-to-gateway VPN leave unprotected?
notes.back: The links between clients and their local gateway, and between the remote gateway and the destination hosts.
notes.explanation: The architecture only protects data between the two gateways; other VPN models cover more of the path.
notes.evidence: the gateway-to-gateway architecture only protects data between the two gateways, as denoted by the solid line. The dashed lines indicate that communications between VPN clients and their local gateway and between the remote gateway and destination hosts (e.g., servers) are not protected by the gateway-to-gateway architecture. The other VPN models provide protection for more of the transit path.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, 2.4.1 Gateway-to-Gateway, PDF p. 29

notes.front: In ESP tunnel mode, what does the new outer IP header name as source and destination?
notes.back: The endpoints of the ESP tunnel, such as two IPsec gateways.
notes.explanation: The whole original packet, now encrypted, becomes the new packet's payload, which is why tunnel mode suits every VPN architecture.
notes.evidence: The new IP header lists the endpoints of the ESP tunnel (such as two IPsec gateways) as the This publication is available free of charge from: https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-77r1 source and destination of the packet and contains the entire, now-encrypted, original packet as its payload. Because of this, tunnel mode can be used with all VPN architectures
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, 4.1.1 Tunnel Mode and Transport Mode, PDF p. 54

notes.front: In ESP transport mode, which IP header is used, and is it integrity-protected?
notes.back: The original IP header is used, and it is not integrity-protected.
notes.explanation: Its overhead is lower than tunnel mode's.
notes.evidence: ESP uses the original IP header instead of creating a new one. The ESP payload and trailer are encrypted, and an ICV is computed over the ESP header and the encrypted data. Integrity protection is not provided for the IP header. The overhead of the transport mode is less than that of the tunnel mode
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, 4.1.1 Tunnel Mode and Transport Mode, PDF p. 54

notes.front: What does the IPsec Authentication Header protocol offer, and what is NIST's view of it?
notes.back: Integrity only, with no confidentiality; NIST discourages its use.
notes.explanation: ESP with null encryption and an integrity algorithm, such as HMAC-SHA-2, achieves the same.
notes.evidence: It offers only integrity algorithms and provides no confidentiality. The ESP protocol can use null encryption (ESP algorithm number 12) with an integrity algorithm, such as HMAC-SHA-2, to accomplish the same as AH.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, 4.4 Authentication Header (AH), PDF p. 62

notes.front: Under SP 800-52 Rev. 2, which TLS version shall servers for government-only applications be configured to use?
notes.back: TLS 1.2, and they should also be configured to use TLS 1.3.
notes.explanation: These servers should not be configured to use TLS 1.1, and shall not use TLS 1.0, SSL 3.0 or SSL 2.0.
notes.evidence: Servers that support government-only applications 8 shall be configured to use TLS 1.2 and should be configured to use TLS 1.3 as well. These servers should not be configured to use TLS 1.1 and shall not use TLS 1.0, SSL 3.0, or SSL 2.0.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-52 Rev. 2, Guidelines for the Selection, Configuration, and Use of TLS Implementations, 3.1 Protocol Version Support, PDF p. 17

notes.front: By what date did SP 800-52 Rev. 2 require agencies to support TLS 1.3?
notes.back: 1 January 2024.
notes.explanation: After that date, servers shall support TLS 1.3 for both government-only and citizen- or business-facing applications.
notes.evidence: Agencies shall support TLS 1.3 by January 1, 2024. After this date, servers shall support TLS 1.3 for both government-only and citizen or business-facing applications.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-52 Rev. 2, Guidelines for the Selection, Configuration, and Use of TLS Implementations, 3.1 Protocol Version Support, PDF p. 17

notes.front: Which SSL versions shall citizen- or business-facing servers not allow, under SP 800-52 Rev. 2?
notes.back: SSL 2.0 and SSL 3.0.
notes.explanation: Such servers may still enable TLS 1.0 or 1.1 where needed to interact with citizens and businesses, but never SSL.
notes.evidence: The use of TLS versions 1.1 and 1.0 is generally discouraged, but these versions may be configured when necessary to enable interaction with citizens and businesses. See Appendix F for a discussion on determining whether to support TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1. These servers shall not allow the use of SSL 2.0 or SSL 3.0.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-52 Rev. 2, Guidelines for the Selection, Configuration, and Use of TLS Implementations, 3.1 Protocol Version Support, PDF p. 17

notes.front: Besides remote login and file transfer, what can SSH do with specific ports?
notes.back: Tunnel them through an SSH connection, letting a local connection reach a remote resource or a remote connection reach a local one.
notes.explanation: SSH is also often used on intermediary hosts, called bastion hosts, to jump to other hosts.
notes.evidence: it can also be used to tunnel specific ports via an SSH connection to allow either a local connection to access a remote resource or a remote connection to access a local resource. SSH is often used on intermediary hosts (also called bastion hosts) to jump to other hosts
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, 8.4 Secure Shell (SSH), PDF p. 107

notes.front: In Fibre Channel over Ethernet, the Fibre Channel frame is {{c1::encapsulated in Ethernet packets}}.
notes.explanation: It is one of the widely deployed storage area network protocols SP 800-209 lists, beside IP-based storage networks such as iSCSI.
notes.evidence: IP SAN is a network stack that uses the IP protocol at the network layer. iSCSI [3] is an example of IP SAN. In FCoE, the Fibre-Channel frame is encapsulated in Ethernet packets.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-209, Security Guidelines for Storage Infrastructure, 2.1 Storage Technologies, PDF p. 16

notes.front: What is north-south traffic, and which traffic do most perimeter security tools focus on?
notes.back: Ingress traffic from outside the local network to endpoints inside it; most perimeter tools focus only on it.
notes.explanation: Firewalls and intrusion detection and prevention systems are the perimeter tools SP 800-215 names.
notes.evidence: most perimeter security solutions (e.g., intrusion prevention system - IPS, intrusion detection systems - IDS, firewalls) focus only on north-south traffic (i.e., ingress, which refers to traffic that originates from outside of the local network and destined for endpoints in the local cluster network).
notes.source: NIST SP 800-215, Guide to a Secure Enterprise Network Landscape, 2 Traditional Network Security Approaches, PDF p. 14

notes.front: According to SP 800-53, how do out-of-band channels compare with in-band channels for exposure?
notes.back: They do not have the same vulnerability or exposure as in-band channels.
notes.explanation: In-band channels are the same channels that carry routine operational traffic.
notes.evidence: The use of out-of-band channels is contrasted with the use of in-band channels (i.e., the same channels) that carry routine operational traffic. Out-of-band channels do not have the same vulnerability or exposure as in-band channels.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, SC-37 Out-of-Band Channels, PDF p. 350

notes.front: Why does SP 800-82 say that relying on air gaps is no longer enough to protect OT systems?
notes.back: OT systems are increasingly being connected to IT networks.
notes.explanation: Security measures tailored to the OT system are therefore needed.
notes.evidence: As OT systems are increasingly being connected to IT networks, relying on traditional measures (e.g., air gaps) is not enough to protect such systems from cyber attacks. Therefore, security measures tailored to the OT system are required to protect the organization.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security, 3.2 Establishing an OT Cybersecurity Program, PDF p. 51

notes.front: In a data centre of physical hosts, how is a VLAN defined?
notes.back: By assigning a unique VLAN tag to switch ports; hosts on those ports join that VLAN, wherever they physically sit.
notes.explanation: That creates a logical grouping of servers within the large flat data centre network.
notes.evidence: a VLAN is defined by assigning a unique ID called a VLAN tag to one or more ports of a physical switch. All hosts connected to those ports then become members of that VLAN ID, creating a logical grouping of servers (hosts), regardless of their physical locations, in the large flat network of a data center.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-125B, Secure Virtual Network Configuration for Virtual Machine (VM) Protection, 2.4 Using VLANs, PDF p. 13

notes.front: Instead of, or as well as, gateway devices, what can an enterprise use to implement micro-segmentation?
notes.back: Host-based micro-segmentation, using software agents or firewalls on the endpoint assets.
notes.explanation: Either way, the gateway devices dynamically grant access to individual requests from a client, asset or service.
notes.evidence: Alternatively (or additionally), the enterprise may choose to implement host-based micro-segmentation using software agents (see Section 3.2.1) or firewalls on the endpoint asset(s), These gateway devices dynamically grant access to individual requests from a client, asset or service.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-207, Zero Trust Architecture, 3.1.2 ZTA Using Micro-Segmentation, PDF p. 21

notes.front: Which outbound traffic should an organisation permit, according to SP 800-41?
notes.back: Only traffic that uses the source IP addresses the organisation actually uses.
notes.explanation: This helps stop traffic with spoofed addresses leaking onto other networks.
notes.evidence: Organizations should only permit outbound traffic that uses the source IP addresses in use by the organization—a process that helps block traffic with spoofed addresses from leaking onto other networks.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, 2.1 Firewall Technologies, PDF p. 13

notes.front: What are the two fundamental components of an 802.11 WLAN?
notes.back: Client devices, such as laptops and smartphones, and access points, which connect them to a distribution system.
notes.explanation: The distribution system is typically the organisation's wired network; some WLANs add wireless switches between access points and it.
notes.evidence: The fundamental components of an IEEE 802.11 WLAN (hereafter referred to as a “WLAN” in this publication) are client devices, such as laptops and smartphones, and access points (APs), which logically connect client devices with a distribution system, typically the organization’s wired network infrastructure. Some WLANs also use wireless switches, which act as intermediaries between APs and the distribution system.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-153, Guidelines for Securing Wireless Local Area Networks (WLANs), Executive Summary, PDF p. 6

notes.front: Why are WLANs typically less secure than wired networks, according to SP 800-153?
notes.back: They are easy to access, and they often have weak security configurations that favour convenience over security.
notes.explanation: Each WLAN's security depends heavily on how well its client devices, access points and wireless switches are secured.
notes.evidence: Unfortunately, WLANs are typically less secure than their wired counterparts for several reasons, including the ease of access to the WLAN and the weak security configurations often used for WLANs (to favor convenience over
notes.source: NIST SP 800-153, Guidelines for Securing Wireless Local Area Networks (WLANs), Executive Summary, PDF p. 6

notes.front: What is a dual-connected client device, and what risk does it bring?
notes.back: A device on a wired network and a WLAN at once; an attacker with wireless access to it could then attack the wired network.
notes.explanation: SP 800-153 asks for policies stating which forms of dual connection are permitted, enforced by security controls.
notes.evidence: The term “dual connected” generally refers to a client device that is connected to both a wired network and a WLAN at the same time. If an attacker gains unauthorized wireless access to a dual-connected client device, the attacker could then use it to access or attack resources on the wired network.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-153, Guidelines for Securing Wireless Local Area Networks (WLANs), Executive Summary, PDF p. 6

notes.front: What should an organisation do if it has more than one security profile for WLAN use, such as guests and staff?
notes.back: Run logically separated WLANs, so devices on one cannot connect to devices on the other.
notes.explanation: SP 800-153 gives external use, such as guests, and internal use as the example pair.
notes.evidence: an organization should have separate WLANs if there is more than one security profile for WLAN usage; for example, an organization should have logically separated WLANs for external use (such as guests) and internal use. Devices on one WLAN should not be able to connect to devices on a logically separated WLAN.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-153, Guidelines for Securing Wireless Local Area Networks (WLANs), Executive Summary, PDF p. 6

notes.front: What is a Bluetooth piconet?
notes.back: Two or more Bluetooth devices close together, operating on the same channel with the same frequency hopping sequence.
notes.explanation: A phone connected to a headset is SP 800-121's example; piconets are often temporary and changing.
notes.evidence: A piconet is composed of two or more Bluetooth devices in close physical proximity that operate on the same channel using the same frequency hopping sequence. An example of a piconet is a connection between a cell phone and a headset using Bluetooth wireless technology. Bluetooth piconets are often established on a temporary and changing basis
notes.source: NIST SP 800-121 Rev. 2 (upd. 1), Guide to Bluetooth Security, 2 Overview of Bluetooth Technology, PDF p. 14

notes.front: Why does SP 800-121 say Bluetooth Security Mode 1 should never be used?
notes.back: Devices in Security Mode 1 never initiate security.
notes.explanation: Security Modes 2 and 4 can use authentication and encryption but start them only after the physical link is fully established.
notes.evidence: Security Modes 2 and 4 can also use authentication and encryption, but do not initiate them until after the Bluetooth physical link has already been fully established and logical channels partially established. Security Mode 1 devices never initiate security and therefore should never be used.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-121 Rev. 2 (upd. 1), Guide to Bluetooth Security, Executive Summary, PDF p. 7

notes.front: What does Bluetooth Security Mode 3 enforce, and when?
notes.back: Authentication and encryption for all connections, started before the physical link is fully established.
notes.explanation: It is the link level-enforced mode, so even service discovery waits until security is in place.
notes.evidence: Security Mode 3 is the link level-enforced security mode, in which a Bluetooth device initiates security procedures before the physical link is fully established. Bluetooth devices operating in Security Mode 3 mandate authentication and encryption for all connections to and from the device. Therefore, even service discovery cannot be performed until after authentication, encryption, and
notes.source: NIST SP 800-121 Rev. 2 (upd. 1), Guide to Bluetooth Security, 3.1 Security Features of Bluetooth BR/EDR/HS, PDF p. 24

notes.front: What is bluesnarfing?
notes.back: An attack that exploits a firmware flaw in older devices to force a Bluetooth connection and reach data stored on the device.
notes.explanation: SP 800-121 dates the vulnerable devices to around 2003.
notes.evidence: Bluesnarfing 32 enables attackers to gain access to a Bluetooth-enabled device by exploiting a firmware flaw in older (circa 2003) devices. This attack forces a connection to a Bluetooth device, allowing access to data stored on the device
notes.source: NIST SP 800-121 Rev. 2 (upd. 1), Guide to Bluetooth Security, 4.1 Bluetooth Vulnerabilities, Threats and Countermeasures, PDF p. 51

notes.front: What is bluejacking?
notes.back: Sending unsolicited messages to the user of a Bluetooth-enabled device.
notes.explanation: The messages do no harm to the device themselves, but may entice the user to respond.
notes.evidence: Bluejacking is an attack conducted on Bluetooth-enabled mobile devices, such as cell phones. An attacker initiates bluejacking by sending unsolicited messages to the user of a Bluetooth-enabled device. The actual messages do not cause harm to the user’s device, but they may entice the user to respond
notes.source: NIST SP 800-121 Rev. 2 (upd. 1), Guide to Bluetooth Security, 4.1 Bluetooth Vulnerabilities, Threats and Countermeasures, PDF p. 52

notes.front: What is a rogue base station in cellular networks?
notes.back: An unlicensed base station, not run by a genuine mobile operator, that broadcasts a network masquerading as a legitimate carrier.
notes.explanation: The hardware to build one can be bought cheaply off the shelf.
notes.evidence: Rogue base stations are unlicensed base stations that are not owned and operated by an authentic MNO. They broadcast a cellular network masquerading as a legitimate carrier network. The necessary hardware to construct these devices can be inexpensively obtained using commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) hardware.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-187, Guide to LTE Security, 4.2 Rogue Base Stations, PDF p. 32

notes.front: How can a rogue base station weaken the security of an LTE user's connection?
notes.back: By broadcasting at high power to force the phone down to an older network generation.
notes.explanation: The second-generation network's cryptographic algorithms for the air interface have significant weaknesses.
notes.evidence: an attacker can force a user to downgrade to either GSM or UMTS. As of the time of this writing, there are no significant, publicly known weaknesses in the cryptographic algorithms used to protect the confidentiality and integrity of the UMTS air interface. Unfortunately, significant weaknesses exist for the 2G GSM cryptographic algorithms
notes.source: NIST SP 800-187, Guide to LTE Security, 4.2.2 Downgrade Attacks, PDF p. 33

notes.front: What technologies can carry an LTE network's backhaul between cell sites and the core?
notes.back: Many, for example microwave, satellite or fibre.
notes.explanation: The cell sites housing the base stations connect to the core network through the backhaul.
notes.evidence: The cell sites that house the eNodeBs connect to the EPC through the backhaul. The backhaul connection can be provided by a multitude of technologies (e.g., microwave, satellite, fiber, etc).
notes.source: NIST SP 800-187, Guide to LTE Security, 2.4 LTE Network Topologies, PDF p. 15

notes.front: What does SDN's easy dynamic reconfiguration of the data plane make possible, according to SP 800-82?
notes.back: Quick isolation of devices, or redirection and duplication of traffic for monitoring and data capture.
notes.explanation: The central controller acts as an abstraction layer, so switches need not be managed one by one.
notes.evidence: The centralized controller acts as an abstraction layer for network programmability, eliminating the need to individually manage each switch within the network. SDN allows for easy dynamic reconfiguration of the data plane, which can in turn allow for the quick isolation of devices or redirection and duplication of traffic for monitoring and data capture.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security, E.1.4 Software-Defined Networking, PDF p. 225

notes.front: Which techniques does SP 800-215 say SD-WAN uses to serve an application's business priority?
notes.back: Bandwidth utilisation, load balancing, and optimising speed by reducing jitter, latency and packet loss.
notes.explanation: Jitter, latency and packet loss are the performance measures the optimisation aims to reduce.
notes.evidence: This capability is enabled using techniques such as bandwidth utilization, load balancing, and the optimization of speed by reducing jitters, latency, and packet loss.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-215, Guide to a Secure Enterprise Network Landscape, 5.3 Secure Access Service Edge, PDF p. 32

notes.front: What do network monitoring and observability tools present, according to SP 800-215?
notes.back: A dashboard of the enterprise network's topography, showing all connections and key operating parameters such as latency and traffic level.
notes.explanation: The tools gather data to give visibility into the entire network.
notes.evidence: This class of tools gathers these data for obtaining visibility into the entire network. These data are then used to generate a dashboard that presents the topography of the enterprise network by showing all connections and presenting key operating parameters (e.g., latency, network traffic- level).
notes.source: NIST SP 800-215, Guide to a Secure Enterprise Network Landscape, 3.4.1 Network Monitoring and Observability Tools, PDF p. 21

notes.front: Bit errors from a noisy cable between two devices are caught and corrected before the data reaches routing. In the OSI model, which layer did that?
notes.back: C) The Data Link Layer.
notes.choices:
A) The Physical Layer
B) The Network Layer
C) The Data Link Layer
D) The Transport Layer
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Physical Layer carries the bits but leaves error detection to the layer above. B: the Network Layer handles routing and relaying. D: the Transport Layer works end to end, above routing.
notes.explanation: Detecting, and possibly correcting, errors that occur in the Physical Layer is a Data Link Layer function.
notes.source: ITU-T Recommendation X.200 (07/1994), Basic Reference Model, 7.6.2 Purpose (Data Link Layer), PDF p. 50
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A filter rule matches on packets' source and destination IP addresses. In the four-layer IP model, at which layer is that information added?
notes.back: B) The network layer.
notes.choices:
A) The application layer
B) The network layer
C) The transport layer
D) The data link layer
notes.choicesExplained: A: application data is produced there, before any addressing. C: transport controls cannot protect IP information because it is added below them. D: the data link layer handles communication between physical components.
notes.explanation: IP information, such as IP addresses, is added at the network layer.
notes.evidence: Another advantage of network layer controls is that since IP information (e.g., IP addresses) is added at this layer
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, 2.1 The Need for Network Layer Security, PDF p. 22

notes.front: A logging database stores addresses in a 32-bit field. The team is adding IPv6 support. How many bits must the field hold for an IPv6 address?
notes.back: 128 bits.
notes.explanation: IPv6 addresses are 128 bits long, four times the 32 bits of an IPv4 address.
notes.evidence: Each IPv6 address is 128 bits long (as defined in RFC 4291)
notes.source: NIST SP 800-119, Guidelines for the Secure Deployment of IPv6, 2.3.1 Extended Address Space, PDF p. 17

notes.front: A new IPv6 host needs to reach every router on its local link with one packet, where an IPv4 host might have broadcast. Which address type does it use?
notes.back: A) Multicast.
notes.choices:
A) Multicast
B) Broadcast
C) Anycast
D) Unicast
notes.choicesExplained: B: IPv6 has eliminated broadcast. C: an anycast packet reaches only one of the interfaces sharing the address. D: a unicast packet reaches a single interface.
notes.explanation: In IPv6, broadcast has been eliminated and multicast has taken over its role.
notes.evidence: In IPv6, broadcast has been eliminated and multicast takes on a much larger role.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-119, Guidelines for the Secure Deployment of IPv6, 4.2 Multicast, PDF p. 68

notes.front: A firm with no IPv6 plans finds staff laptops tunnelling IPv6 traffic out through its firewall. What does SP 800-119 recommend?
notes.back: Block all IPv6 traffic, native and tunnelled, in both directions at the firewall.
notes.explanation: That is SP 800-119's recommendation for organisations not yet deploying IPv6.
notes.evidence: Block all IPv6 traffic, native and tunneled, at the organization's firewall. Both incoming and outgoing traffic should be blocked.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-119, Guidelines for the Secure Deployment of IPv6, Executive Summary, PDF p. 11

notes.front: An agency must protect all traffic between two offices, used by dozens of applications, without modifying any of them. Which kind of control fits best?
notes.back: A) A network layer control such as IPsec.
notes.choices:
A) A network layer control such as IPsec
B) Application layer controls built into each application
C) TLS added to each application
notes.choicesExplained: B: each application would need changing, which the agency wants to avoid. C: TLS typically requires each application to support it.
notes.explanation: Network layer controls can protect all communications between two networks without modifying the applications on clients or servers.
notes.evidence: Controls at this layer apply to all applications and are not application- specific. For example, all network communications between two hosts or networks can be protected at this layer without modifying any applications on the clients or the servers.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, 2.1 The Need for Network Layer Security, PDF p. 22

notes.front: Sales staff working from hotels need protected access to their company's internal email and web servers. Which VPN architecture fits?
notes.back: C) Remote access (host-to-gateway).
notes.choices:
A) Gateway-to-gateway
B) Host-to-host
C) Remote access (host-to-gateway)
notes.choicesExplained: A: gateway-to-gateway joins two whole networks, not roaming individual hosts. B: host-to-host protects traffic between two specific computers only.
notes.explanation: Remote access is most often used to let hosts on unsecured networks, such as travelling staff, reach internal organisational services.
notes.evidence: The remote access architecture is most often used to allow hosts on unsecured networks, such as traveling employees and telecommuters, to gain access to internal organizational services, such as the organization’s email and web servers.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, Executive Summary, PDF p. 8

notes.front: Two IPsec gateways link a head office and a branch over the internet. Observers must not learn which internal hosts are talking or which ports they use. Which ESP mode fits?
notes.back: A) Tunnel mode.
notes.choices:
A) Tunnel mode
B) Transport mode
notes.choicesExplained: B: transport mode keeps the original IP header, so the real source and destination stay visible.
notes.explanation: Tunnel mode encrypts the original IP header, concealing the actual source and destination, protocol and ports.
notes.evidence: encrypting the original IP header conceals the nature of the communications, such as the actual source or destination of the packet, protocol, and ports used that would indicate which application is likely being used.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, 4.1.1 Tunnel Mode and Transport Mode, PDF p. 54

notes.front: A team needs IPsec traffic protected for integrity but not confidentiality, and proposes the Authentication Header. What does SP 800-77 advise instead?
notes.back: B) ESP with null encryption and an integrity algorithm.
notes.choices:
A) The Authentication Header, as proposed
B) ESP with null encryption and an integrity algorithm
C) ESP with encryption and no integrity algorithm
notes.choicesExplained: A: NIST discourages the Authentication Header. C: that gives confidentiality, which is not what the team asked for, and omits the integrity it needs.
notes.explanation: ESP with null encryption and an integrity algorithm achieves what the Authentication Header does, and NIST discourages the header.
notes.evidence: The ESP protocol can use null encryption (ESP algorithm number 12) with an integrity algorithm, such as HMAC-SHA-2, to accomplish the same as AH. Alternatively, ESP can use an AEAD algorithm, such as AES-GMAC (ESP algorithm number 21), to offer integrity without confidentiality to replace AH. NIST discourages the use of AH in this publication.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, 4.4 Authentication Header (AH), PDF p. 62

notes.front: Two mail relays exchange messages over TLS. A manager says this guarantees neither relay can alter a message's content. Is the manager right?
notes.back: A) No: TLS protects the transport, not the content from either relay.
notes.choices:
A) No: TLS protects the transport, not the content from either relay
B) Yes: TLS protects everything carried inside it
notes.choicesExplained: B: a TLS link gives transport security only; it does not stop one of the endpoints manipulating the message.
notes.explanation: The transport layer can only provide transport security, not data origin security.
notes.evidence: The transport layer can only provide transport security, not data origin security.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, 2.1 The Need for Network Layer Security, PDF p. 21

notes.front: In 2025, an agency's citizen-facing web server offers TLS 1.2 and SSL 3.0 but not TLS 1.3. Under SP 800-52 Rev. 2, what must change?
notes.back: A) Disable SSL 3.0 and add TLS 1.3 support.
notes.choices:
A) Disable SSL 3.0 and add TLS 1.3 support
B) Disable TLS 1.2 and keep SSL 3.0 for old clients
C) Nothing: TLS 1.2 alone is compliant
notes.choicesExplained: C: servers shall support TLS 1.3 after 1 January 2024, and SSL 3.0 is not allowed. B: SSL 3.0 shall not be allowed, whatever the clients.
notes.explanation: Such servers shall not allow SSL 2.0 or 3.0, and agencies had to support TLS 1.3 by 1 January 2024.
notes.evidence: These servers shall not allow the use of SSL 2.0 or SSL 3.0. Agencies shall support TLS 1.3 by January 1, 2024.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-52 Rev. 2, Guidelines for the Selection, Configuration, and Use of TLS Implementations, 3.1 Protocol Version Support, PDF p. 17

notes.front: An administrator at home must reach a database port on an internal server, going through a bastion host over an encrypted connection. Which tool fits?
notes.back: A) SSH port tunnelling.
notes.choices:
A) SSH port tunnelling
B) An air gap
C) Egress filtering
notes.choicesExplained: B: an air gap removes the connection altogether. C: egress filtering restricts outbound traffic; it does not carry the session.
notes.explanation: SSH can tunnel specific ports so a local connection reaches a remote resource, and is often used on bastion hosts to jump to other hosts.
notes.evidence: it can also be used to tunnel specific ports via an SSH connection to allow either a local connection to access a remote resource or a remote connection to access a local resource. SSH is often used on intermediary hosts (also called bastion hosts) to jump to other hosts
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, 8.4 Secure Shell (SSH), PDF p. 107

notes.front: A company runs block storage traffic over its ordinary IP network, and its servers see the remote disks as if locally attached. What is it using?
notes.back: A) A converged protocol such as iSCSI.
notes.choices:
A) A converged protocol such as iSCSI
B) An overlay network
C) Out-of-band management
notes.choicesExplained: B: an overlay network isolates virtual machine traffic by encapsulation; it is not a storage protocol. C: out-of-band management is about separate administration paths.
notes.explanation: iSCSI runs storage traffic over TCP/IP, and networked storage presents remote devices as if locally attached.
notes.evidence: iSCSI by design running over Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol (TCP/IP), Fibre-Channel over IP [FCIP], Fibre-Channel over Ethernet (FCoE), cloud block storage). In networked storage, the remote storage devices are presented as if they are locally attached to the host system
notes.source: NIST SP 800-209, Security Guidelines for Storage Infrastructure, 2.1 Storage Technologies, PDF p. 15

notes.front: Two microservices in the same data centre call each other thousands of times a minute. How is this traffic classed?
notes.back: B) East-west traffic.
notes.choices:
A) North-south traffic
B) East-west traffic
notes.choicesExplained: A: north-south traffic comes from outside the local network to endpoints inside it.
notes.explanation: Traffic within the local network, or server to server because applications are built from microservices, is east-west.
notes.evidence: over 75 % of network traffic is now east-west (i.e., within the local network) or server-to-server (due to applications being based on microservices)
notes.source: NIST SP 800-215, Guide to a Secure Enterprise Network Landscape, 2 Traditional Network Security Approaches, PDF p. 14

notes.front: A bank's engineers administer its core routers only through a physically separate network that carries no customer or business traffic. What is this?
notes.back: B) Out-of-band management.
notes.choices:
A) East-west traffic
B) Out-of-band management
C) A virtual private cloud
notes.choicesExplained: A: east-west describes traffic within the local network, not a separate administration path. C: a virtual private cloud is a customer network inside a cloud provider.
notes.explanation: Network paths physically separate from those used for operational traffic are out-of-band channels.
notes.evidence: network paths physically separate from network paths used for operational traffic
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, SC-37 Out-of-Band Channels, PDF p. 350

notes.front: A plant cannot afford separate switches for its engineering and office computers, so it splits one switch's ports into two logical groups. What has it built?
notes.back: C) Two VLANs.
notes.choices:
A) An air gap
B) Two SD-WAN sites
C) Two VLANs
notes.choicesExplained: A: an air gap means no connection at all, not a shared switch. B: SD-WAN concerns wide area links between sites.
notes.explanation: VLANs logically separate areas of a network by switch port when physical separation is not feasible because of cost.
notes.evidence: A VLAN can be used to logically separate areas within a network when physical separation may not be feasible due to cost or other prohibitive measures.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security, E.1.3 Virtual Local Area Networks, PDF p. 224

notes.front: Each payroll server is placed on its own network segment behind a gateway that decides on every individual request to it. What approach is this?
notes.back: B) Micro-segmentation.
notes.choices:
A) A VLAN only
B) Micro-segmentation
C) Egress filtering
notes.choicesExplained: A: a VLAN groups hosts by switch port but does not by itself decide on each request. C: egress filtering screens outgoing traffic.
notes.explanation: Placing resources on their own segment behind a gateway that dynamically grants individual requests is micro-segmentation.
notes.evidence: An enterprise may choose to implement a ZTA based on placing individual or groups of resources on a unique network segment protected by a gateway security component.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-207, Zero Trust Architecture, 3.1.2 ZTA Using Micro-Segmentation, PDF p. 21

notes.front: Firewall logs show outbound packets carrying source addresses the organisation does not own. What should the firewall do?
notes.back: Block them: that is egress filtering.
notes.explanation: Outbound traffic with invalid source addresses should be blocked, which is often called egress filtering.
notes.evidence: Outbound traffic with invalid source addresses should be blocked (this is often called egress filtering).
notes.source: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, 4.1 Policies Based on IP Addresses and Protocols, PDF p. 29

notes.front: A hotel runs guests and back-office staff on one WLAN, and guests' laptops can see the staff printers. What does SP 800-153 recommend?
notes.back: Logically separated WLANs for guests and for internal use, with no connections between them.
notes.explanation: More than one security profile calls for separate WLANs, and devices on one should not reach devices on the other.
notes.evidence: an organization should have logically separated WLANs for external use (such as guests) and internal use. Devices on one WLAN should not be able to connect to devices on a logically separated WLAN.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-153, Guidelines for Securing Wireless Local Area Networks (WLANs), Executive Summary, PDF p. 6

notes.front: In a café, an attacker exploits a firmware flaw in an old phone to force a Bluetooth connection and copy data stored on it. Which attack is this?
notes.back: B) Bluesnarfing.
notes.choicesExplained: A: bluejacking only sends unsolicited messages; it does not take data from the device.
notes.explanation: Bluesnarfing forces a connection through a firmware flaw in older devices and gives access to stored data.
notes.evidence: Bluesnarfing 32 enables attackers to gain access to a Bluetooth-enabled device by exploiting a firmware flaw in older (circa 2003) devices. This attack forces a connection to a Bluetooth device, allowing access to data stored on the device
notes.source: NIST SP 800-121 Rev. 2 (upd. 1), Guide to Bluetooth Security, 4.1 Bluetooth Vulnerabilities, Threats and Countermeasures, PDF p. 51

notes.front: Near a protest, many phones suddenly drop from LTE to an old second-generation network, after a strong nearby transmitter starts posing as their carrier. What is happening?
notes.back: A) A downgrade attack by a rogue base station.
notes.choices:
A) A downgrade attack by a rogue base station
B) Bluejacking
C) Backhaul eavesdropping
notes.choicesExplained: B: bluejacking sends unsolicited Bluetooth messages. C: backhaul eavesdropping taps links between cell sites and the core, not the phones' radio link.
notes.explanation: A rogue base station broadcasting at high power can force users down to older networks whose algorithms are weaker.
notes.evidence: Using a rogue base station broadcasting at a high power level, an attacker can force a user to downgrade to either GSM or UMTS.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-187, Guide to LTE Security, 4.2.2 Downgrade Attacks, PDF p. 33

notes.front: A security team wants to isolate an infected device within seconds and mirror its traffic to a monitoring tool, by reprogramming forwarding from one central point. Which technology supports this?
notes.back: C) Software-defined networking.
notes.choices:
A) An air gap
B) A content distribution network
C) Software-defined networking
notes.choicesExplained: A: an air gap is a fixed absence of connection, not something reprogrammed on the fly. B: a content distribution network serves cached copies of content.
notes.explanation: SDN's dynamic reconfiguration of the data plane allows quick isolation of devices and duplication of traffic for monitoring.
notes.evidence: SDN allows for easy dynamic reconfiguration of the data plane, which can in turn allow for the quick isolation of devices or redirection and duplication of traffic for monitoring and data capture.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security, E.1.4 Software-Defined Networking, PDF p. 225

notes.front: According to RFC 1122, the Internet application layer does the work of which OSI layers?
notes.back: The top two: Presentation (layer 6) and Application (layer 7).
notes.explanation: Where OSI splits this work into two layers, the Internet suite keeps a single application layer, even if particular protocols layer themselves internally.
notes.source: RFC 1122, Requirements for Internet Hosts: Communication Layers, 1.1.3 Internet Protocol Suite (Application Layer), page 9
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How do the address types used by IPv4 and IPv6 differ?
notes.back: IPv4 uses unicast, multicast and broadcast. IPv6 drops broadcast and uses unicast, multicast and anycast.
notes.explanation: SP 800-119's comparison table lists broadcast as no longer used in IPv6.
notes.evidence: use of unicast, multicast, and broadcast addressing no longer broadcast address types used, use of unicast, multicast and anycast address types
notes.source: NIST SP 800-119, Guidelines for the Secure Deployment of IPv6, Table 2-1 IPv4 and IPv6 comparison, PDF p. 23

notes.front: How does ESP tunnel mode differ from transport mode in what it protects?
notes.back: Tunnel mode encrypts and integrity-protects the original IP header too; transport mode keeps the original header unprotected.
notes.explanation: Tunnel mode wraps the whole original packet under a new header; transport mode reuses the original header, so it has less overhead.
notes.evidence: tunnel mode can encrypt and protect the integrity of both the data and the original IP header for each packet.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, 4.1.1 Tunnel Mode and Transport Mode, PDF p. 54

notes.front: In traditional networking, which plane forwards packets and which runs the routing algorithms?
notes.back: The data plane forwards packets; the control plane runs the distributed algorithms that determine routing.
notes.explanation: Traditional switches carry out both; SDN moves the control plane to a central controller.
notes.evidence: Traditional networking switches are responsible for both forwarding packets (data plane) and running the distributed algorithms that determine routing (control plane).
notes.source: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security, E.1.4 Software-Defined Networking, PDF p. 225

notes.front: Why does SP 800-125B call overlay-based segmentation much more scalable than VLAN-based segmentation?
notes.back: The overlay segment identifier is 24 bits against the VLAN's 12, giving about 16 million segments instead of 4096.
notes.explanation: The overlay's encapsulating packet is an IP and User Datagram Protocol packet.
notes.evidence: is a 24-bit field compared to the 12-bit VLAN ID. Hence the namespace for VXLANs (and the number of network segments that can be created) is about 16 million as opposed to 4096 for VLANs. (b) The encapsulating packet for overlay-based network segmentation is an IP/User Datagram Protocol (UDP) packet.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-125B, Secure Virtual Network Configuration for Virtual Machine (VM) Protection, 2.5.1 Advantages, PDF p. 17

notes.front: How do OT and IT systems typically differ on delay, jitter and throughput, according to SP 800-82?
notes.back: OT is time-critical, with limits on delay and jitter, and rarely needs high throughput; IT needs high throughput and tolerates some delay and jitter.
notes.explanation: In OT, the acceptable levels of delay and jitter are set by each installation.
notes.evidence: OT systems are generally time-critical, with the criterion for acceptable levels of delay and jitter dictated by the individual installation. Some systems require reliable, deterministic responses. High throughput is typically not essential to OT. In contrast, IT systems typically require high throughput and can withstand some level of delay and jitter.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security, 2.4 Comparing OT and IT System Security, PDF p. 46
